extracted.intended_audience: young readers and their educators (governesses); general readers interested in writing/teaching history for children
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance (Victorian/Ruskinian) for composing moral, accessible sketches of history for boys and girls: emphasise virtue and Providence, use illustrative devices (maps/plates), avoid sensationalism and anachronistic or partisan explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: History as praise / faithful history
rubrics_metrics.description: "all great Art is Praise. So is all faithful History, and all high Philosophy." (Ruskin's assertion about the proper tone and purpose of history and art.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History should praise and highlight virtue rather than dwell on vice; faithful history shares the same moral/affirming aim as great art and philosophy. Avoid a cynical or purely destructive tone; let history show what is worthy of praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: True knowledge concerns virtues only
rubrics_metrics.description: "For true knowledge is of Virtues only; of poisons and vices, it is Hecate who teaches, not Athena."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or writing history, foreground the knowledge of virtues and their effects. Do not treat immoral deeds as the central educational subject-matter; do not glorify vice or present corruption as the main lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: History should be edifying and accessible to pupils
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin was asked to "write some pieces of history which her pupils could gather some good out of;--the fruit of historical documents placed by modern educational systems at her disposal, being to them labour only, and sorrow."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose historical pieces so that young students can "gather some good"—make material morally instructive and readable rather than tedious. Adapt documents and narratives to be intelligible and uplifting for children under a governess' instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensational, Newgate-Calendar style history
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the Lear-paraphrase example, Ruskin criticizes popular history that reads like a catalogue of crimes and brutal incidents which corrupt the mind: such histories are "about as profitable reading for young persons ... as the Newgate Calendar would be."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not structure history as lurid anecdotes of crime and scandal. Avoid sensational woodcuts and graphic recitals of wrongdoing that undermine respect for institutions or present moral chaos; instead select material that cultivates respect and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Providence and the virtue of men as history's profitable truths
rubrics_metrics.description: "Meantime, the two ignored powers--the Providence of Heaven, and the virtue of men--have ruled, and rule, the world... they are the only powers of which history has ever to tell any profitable truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing themes and explanations, highlight Providence and human virtue as the central forces worth recounting; resist reducing history to mechanics of politics or economics alone. Emphasize moral causes and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pedagogical devices (maps, sketches, plates) to teach geography and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin instructs the reader: "Sketch for yourself, first, a map of France..." and includes plates and plans—he uses visual/active exercises as part of teaching history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ maps, diagrams, plates, and directed exercises to make spatial and chronological relations clear to learners. Ask readers to draw or copy simple maps/figures to internalize context and retain narrative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anachronistic or simplistic modern judgments of historical actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin rebukes the "cockney historian" who reduces Clovis's conversion to mere policy: "The cockney historian had better limit his remarks ... Frankish kings were made of other clay."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret historical characters in the light of their own cultural and moral context rather than imposing modern assumptions. Be cautious of facile causal explanations (e.g., 'conversion was political') that ignore contemporaneous mentalities and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach virtue by example and deeds rather than sermonizing
rubrics_metrics.description: On St. Martin: "the especial character of St. Martin is a serene and meek charity ... He is not a preaching saint ... What he does always, is merely the right thing at the right moment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray exemplary figures through narratives of concrete actions that exhibit virtues quietly and practically. Use life-stories that show virtue in practice rather than long moralizing passages; let actions instruct the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve respect for institutions; do not let history erode civic faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin warns that sensational or purely scandalous history "overthrows his respect for any manner of government, and his faith in the ordinances of Providence itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting episodes, provide context that prevents wholesale cynicism about institutions. Balance critical accounts with recognition of stabilizing, virtuous elements so readers retain a sense of social order and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce history to narrow partisan or utilitarian lenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin criticizes histories by "bankers, members of Parliament, or orthodox clergymen" that assert civilization consists in "the victory of usury" or the "establishment of the Parliamentary privileges" etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating histories whose sole thesis is an economic, sectarian, or single-interest triumph. Aim for broad moral and human perspectives rather than narrowly arguing that one social interest explains all historical change.
